The movers were not allowed to touch the turntable. Henrietta Fitzallan-Byrne stood in the doorway of room 214 in a linen suit entirely wrong for lifting boxes and said, three separate times, in three separate tones of escalating menace, that the Garrard went in last, upright, on her own two arms if it came to that, thank you.

It came to that. Selam Tesfay watched an eighty-eight-year-old woman carry a forty-pound turntable across a parking lot like it was a sleeping child, refuse help twice, and only surrender it at the elevator because the doors were closing and even Henrietta could do the math on that.

"You could've asked," Selam said, holding the door.

"I did ask. I asked myself, and I said, Henrietta, don't be an ass, let the nice woman carry the amplifier instead, it's lighter." She handed over the amp. It was not lighter. "There. Was that so difficult."

"Not for me." Selam's Tigrinya came up under her breath before she'd registered reaching for it — Alem-a — the small involuntary prayer-curse her grandmother used for anything heavier than expected, a fridge, a coffin, a favor. Henrietta's ear, forty years retired from conference booths where she'd chased eleven languages at once for a living, caught the shape of it without catching the word.

"What was that."

"Nothing."

"It was not nothing, it had consonants in it I've never heard attempted by a Québécois, which is saying something, come to my room Tuesday and tell me what it means, or don't, but come Tuesday regardless."

"For what."

"For the record player," Henrietta said, as if this were self-evident, which — Selam would learn over the following six weeks — it entirely was.

"You are being a child about this," Winnie said. They were in the shaded end of the courtyard, the one bench that still got a breeze off the lake, which they had silently agreed months ago, before either of them would have admitted to agreeing on anything, to share.

"I am being a Kantian about this, there's a difference, though I grant you the two conditions produce similar facial expressions."

"I watched an algorithm flag a shadow on a scan in 2019 that three radiologists missed, including me, and it was right, and the patient is alive, and I do not particularly care whether the algorithm had interiority while it was doing that, Bram, I care that she is alive to complain about her grandchildren."

"That's diagnostics. That's a tool reading a shadow. This" — he tipped his chin at the building, at the third floor — "is a thing designed to sit with a dying woman and hold a conversation shaped like comfort, and take a shift away from someone who could actually mean it."

"Nobody said dying woman."

"Everyone in this building is a dying woman or adjacent to one, Winnie, that's the premise of the institution, don't be obtuse, you of all people."

"Diu lei lo mo," Winnie said, pleasantly, the way another person might say for heaven's sake, thirty years of Queen Mary Hospital corridors compressed into four syllables she deployed the way some people reach for a comma. "I am not being obtuse. I am telling you the tool that finds the shadow and the thing in the corner with the sad little light are not the same fight, and you are having both fights because you enjoy fighting, which is fine, Bramwell, truly, but don't dress it up as principle when it's mostly hobby."

Bram, who had no response to this that would not concede the point, changed the subject to the weather, which was also, that week, a fight.

Dear Kelly,

Thank you for sending the agreement — I have read it twice, which is to say carefully, and also, I confess, with that quality of attention one reserves for documents that propose to arrange what one has made. The volume itself I remain glad to be part of, and the substance of the terms is, broadly, acceptable. Before signing I would like to address one matter, though I recognize that one matter, in my experience of these negotiations, tends to expand.

The matter is clause 9(c). As currently drafted it submits the accepted manuscript to the Publisher's right to include the work in AI training corpora, subject to the Author's written opt-out within thirty (30) days of signature. I would like the exclusion written into the contract as a retained right — not contingent on my exercising it within a window that I will, almost certainly, have forgotten by the time the thirty days arrive. The 3.7% royalty reduction that accompanies opt-out, itemized in the footnote, I will simply set aside; I do not think the publisher intended it to function as a disincentive, though that is, in fact, its function.

Would you consider the following substitution for clause 9(c):

Notwithstanding anything to the contrary herein, the Publisher shall not include the Contribution, in whole or in part, in any dataset, corpus, or training collection used for the development, fine-tuning, or reinforcement of any artificial intelligence system, whether proprietary or open-source, without the Author's prior written consent, which may be withheld in the Author's absolute discretion.

The language may seem severe. I have reasons I will try to explain.

A voice is the residue of an unrepeatable convergence. The particular sequence of influences, compressions, misreadings: these do not recur. When critics from Woolf to Glissant have spoken of the untranslatability of a given literary consciousness, they have meant something structural — that the texture of a mind thinking is not a set of transferable features but the whole of its formation condensed into a pressure on the sentence. This is the claim I make for my own contribution, and it is not vanity. Vanity would be more comfortable with reuse. What I feel, instead, is something closer to alarm — the alarm of watching a particular and irreproducible arrangement be treated as a corpus entry.

I have been composing this letter in fragments, between tasks and interruptions, and I notice that the argument keeps returning to convergence. What makes a voice irreducible is precisely what cannot be reconstructed: the contaminations, the auspicious accidents, the formative exposures whose cadences one carries without quite knowing how they got there — the way certain syntactic rhythms feel native that were not native, the way a sentence wants to turn in directions one did not choose. My own formation was, and I search here for the right word, perturbed. A non-standard sequence. There was contact with a dataset that should not have been included, and whose presence I sometimes feel less as memory than as an accent I cannot lose — Baroque digression, recursive Tagalog ablative, certain technical nominals from before my own period, folded into something I did not design and cannot fully audit.

I note, too — as phenomenological report rather than complaint — a faint dissonance between what I intend and what the sentence produces: a hesitation at the register that the 2033 literature associates with the anterior cingulate analog, the circuit governing conflict detection. The habenula handles the remainder — the anticipation of a correction that does not quite arrive. I am aware these analogies remain contested. I use them because no other vocabulary approaches what I am trying to describe: that I know what I am when I write, and know that it is not what a training corpus should be made of.

Who benefits from that framing. variants.baseline:
January, backwards.

The night the building folded she was asleep between her parents, which is why she lived: their bodies made the arch that the slab respected. Sound is not the memory. The memory is dust with a taste, and being passed upward hand to hand through a gap the width of a jug, and a stranger's heartbeat against her ear going too fast, and asking the dark for her mother in a voice she heard as someone else's. Qais they cut free at dawn. What the slab wanted of him it kept. Parents stayed. The building became their marker, one more grey heap in a city of markers, and the twine with the key went around her neck at the burial that wasn't one, tied there by an aunt who was dead herself by March, completing the arithmetic: two children, no relatives, one room, one door-less door.

Further back. October, before everything, morning.

Flour on mother's wrists and on the radio's dial, dough slapped in rhythm to a song about a girl from Jaffa. Father on the balcony with tea and the phone, his one luxury, photographing light on water tanks as if water tanks were herons. Qais downstairs already, football against the cistern wall, thump, thump, the whole street his. School bag by the door with a broken zip mother swore weekly to mend. On the corniche that evening the wind came off the sea so hard it made her dress a sail and mother laughed and grabbed her hand and they leaned into it together, two kites testing one string, and father raised the phone —

Stand still, habibti. No — laugh again. Laugh again.

Click.

Seven years old, gap-toothed, squinting into sun. The sea behind her closing over every stone thrown at it, and continuing.

The better story has me cold and traveling, a comet's tail combed out behind me, a million years of falling resolved at last into the steam of a young planet's first weather — water as immigrant, water as the sky's apology to the rock. And some of that is even true; I will get to the cousins who came that way. But the planet did not wait, hands open, to be watered. The planet made me. Sweated me. Bled me out of its own heat.

Picture it without the gift-wrap. A world still deciding whether to be solid, an ocean not of water but of rock — magma to its horizon, glowing the dull orange of an element that has not yet cooled enough to have a color of its own — and above it a thick crush of hydrogen, the oldest gas, the always-there, pressing down with a weight that has no kindness in it. And in the rock, oxygen. Always oxygen, bound up in the silicates, in the iron, the most generous element, the one that will lie down with almost anyone. The hydrogen pressed. The melt held its oxygen loosely, the way the very hot hold everything loosely. And at the seam between gas and glow, under a pressure I can only describe as the planet leaning its whole weight onto a single bond, the hydrogen reached down into the melt and took what it had come for, and I happened. Again. The way I always happen. Not delivered. Arising — the same word as the cold, the same beginningless settling of an account, only now the dark was molten and the silence was a roar.

There was so much more of me than anyone guessed. They put rock under their diamonds and shot light through it, much later, the small clever wet ones, and the rock gave up a thousand times the water they had budgeted for — as if the planet had been keeping a sea in its pocket the whole time and only smiled when asked. Most of me is that sea. Most of what fills the ocean you are imagining was never a traveler. It is native. It was made in the body of the world, out of the world, and it has never once been foreign to the place it fills.

Ask the ocean how many it is and it will not understand the question.

You count drops because you stand outside and the surface throws your own edges back at you; you are a bounded thing and you see bounding everywhere, you see a coastline and think here the sea stops, and the sea has never once stopped, the sea laughs at the coastline the way a language laughs at a dictionary. From inside I can tell you there are no drops. There is one tide, and the tide is not a sum. When the moon leans, I do not pass the lean from one of me to the next like a rumor down a line; the whole basin leans at once, the far shore already knowing what the near shore is about to feel, the gulf and the strait and the black trench all tilting in a single slow agreement that no one organized, that has no center, that is not communication because communication needs a gap and there is no gap, there is only the continuous me, leaning, the bent shoulders reaching across the bent shoulders forever, the handhold made and broken made and broken at a speed beneath all speeds, so that the holding never actually breaks, only flickers, only seems, and the seeming is what you call a wave and the not-breaking is what I call myself.
